body.x: Every Shia marriage begins with a short exchange of Arabic sentences. They take less than a minute to say, yet they are the marriage: before them, two people are non-mahram to each other; after them, husband and wife. That exchange is the seegha — also written sigha — the formula of offer (ijab) and acceptance (qabul). Because the words do so much, couples understandably want to know exactly what is said, what it means, and how to be sure it is said correctly. This page sets out the standard wording as printed in the practical law books of the marjas, with transliteration and translation. It is an educational guide, not a substitute for an officiant: the wording used at your nikah should follow your own marja's manual and the scholar conducting the ceremony.
Why a handful of words carries the whole marriage

In Shia fiqh a marriage is a contract — an 'aqd — and like any contract it is formed by an offer and an acceptance. What makes the nikah distinctive is that the offer and acceptance are spoken in a set form, in Arabic, in one sitting, with the mahr specified. There is no separate legal moment hidden elsewhere — not the signing, not the celebration, not the civil registration, important as those are. If the seegha is recited correctly, by the couple or by representatives they have authorised, with free consent on both sides, the marriage exists. That is why families take the wording seriously, why the officiant confirms the names and the mahr before beginning, and why, if a word is stumbled over, the formula is repeated rather than shrugged off.
When the bride and groom recite it themselves
A couple may recite the seegha directly, without representatives. In the form printed in the law books, the bride speaks first, offering herself in marriage; the groom answers with his acceptance:

Bride: Ankahtu-ka nafsi 'ala al-mahr al-ma'lum.
Groom: Qabiltu al-nikah.

Take the bride's sentence apart. Ankahtu-ka means 'I marry to you' — the verb is in the past tense because the contract is concluded by the speaking, not promised for some later time. Nafsi is 'myself': she is giving herself in marriage, in person, not being handed over by anyone else. 'Ala al-mahr al-ma'lum means 'for the specified mahr' — al-ma'lum, 'the known one', points to the mahr the two sides have already discussed, agreed and fixed; the contract does not invent it on the spot. The groom's reply is as short as Arabic allows: Qabiltu al-nikah, 'I accept the marriage.' The acceptance must follow the offer in the same sitting, in words that clearly take up this offer — an acceptance spoken hours later, or in reply to something else, does not complete the contract.
When representatives recite it: the wakil form

More often, each side appoints a wakil — a representative, frequently the officiating scholar acting for one or both parties with their explicit permission. The wording shifts into the third person, because the wakil is speaking about his client, not about himself. The bride's wakil addresses the groom in words of this pattern: 'Ankahtu-ka muwakkilati [her name] 'ala al-mahr al-ma'lum' — 'I marry my client, [name], to you for the specified mahr.' If the groom answers in person, he may say 'Qabiltu hadha al-nikah' — 'I accept this marriage.' If he too has a wakil, the acceptance runs: 'Qabiltu hadha al-nikah li-muwakkili [his name]' — 'I accept this marriage on behalf of my client, [name].' Notice what the wakil form adds: names. Each party is identified precisely, so there can be no doubt about who is being married to whom — one reason the officiant asks for full names in advance and has them written down before the ceremony begins.
The small variations you will see in print

Read two law books side by side and you may notice differences. Some print zawwajtuka where others print ankahtuka; both verbs carry the sense of giving in marriage and both appear in the manuals. Some wordings say 'ala al-sadaq al-ma'lum, using sadaq — another word for the bridal gift — where others say mahr. A manual may also set out the wording for the case where one person acts as wakil for both sides, which is permitted when both parties have authorised him. These are variations inside a well-mapped landscape, not contradictions. But they are exactly why a couple should settle beforehand which manual their officiant is following, rather than mixing lines from different books — or from the internet — on the day itself.
Getting the Arabic right on the day

Three practical points follow. First, pronunciation matters: the formula should be recited in correct Arabic by someone able to say it properly, which is why most families ask a scholar or an experienced reciter to lead it, even when the couple could manage an approximation. Second, preparation matters: names, the exact mahr and any agreed conditions should reach the officiant in writing before the ceremony, and many couples quietly listen to the wording in advance so the moment feels familiar rather than daunting. Third, authority matters: if anything about your situation is unusual — a party who cannot attend, a question about representation, a bride whose guardian situation is complicated — put it to your marja's office or a qualified scholar in advance. A two-minute question beforehand protects the very centre of the wedding.

Learn the words by all means. Knowing that ankahtu-ka nafsi means 'I marry myself to you' turns a half-heard ritual into a sentence you understand at the moment it changes your life. Then let the officiant carry the recitation, follow the wording your marja prescribes — and listen to your marriage being spoken into being.
